title: Make a Fossil Print: Parent Guide
endLine: Fossil prints save shapes that reveal past life and places.

scenes.tts: How can a dent in clay show what lived somewhere millions of years ago? In about thirty minutes at your table, you and your child make fossil prints. Together, you turn those prints into clues.
scenes.caption: How can a dent in clay show what lived somewhere millions of years ago? In about thirty minutes at your table, you and your child make fossil prints. Together, you turn those prints into clues.
scenes.visual: Friendly schematic overhead drawing of a newspaper-covered tabletop filling the frame. A ridged scallop shell presses straight down into a flat disc of soft terracotta clay on a paper plate, then lifts straight up, leaving a crisp hollow print. Short high-contrast label: 'Hollow print = mold'. Slow drifting dust motes keep the frame gently alive.
scenes.narration: How can a dent in clay show what lived somewhere millions of years ago? In about thirty minutes at your table, you and your child make fossil prints. Together, you turn those prints into clues.

scenes.tts: This activity gives your child hands-on practice looking closely at small details. They match ridges, leaf veins, and footprints to real objects. They also practice making a guess and checking it against clues. Older kids can practice patience waiting for a cast.

scenes.visual: Same tabletop world, now showing three paper plates holding clay discs with prints of a ridged shell, a veined leaf, and toy animal footprints. A simple schematic magnifying glass glides smoothly across each print, highlighting ridges, veins, and toes with soft glowing rings. Labels: 'Look closely' and 'Guess and check'.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child the whole time. Keep all small objects away from children under four. Cover the table with newspaper. Use store-bought modeling clay that stays soft. Skip homemade flour dough. Gather empty, clean shells with smooth edges, a pinecone, and toy animals. Discard cracked shells. Choose leaves from plants you know and avoid poison ivy. Never taste plants or clay.

scenes.visual: Show the adult covering the tabletop with newspaper. During the under-four warning, show the adult securing the small materials in a closed container out of a younger child's reach. After the warning, show the modeling clay, paper plate, empty smooth shell, leaf, pinecone, and toy animal laid out for the activity with the adult present.

scenes.tts: Have your child knead an orange-sized ball of clay until it softens. Use a rolling pin or smooth plastic jar. Flatten the clay on a paper plate until it is about two centimeters thick. Press the shell straight down, then lift it straight up. That hollow print is a mold.

scenes.visual: Zoom in on a paper plate. Show hands kneading an orange-sized ball of clay and flattening it with a rolling pin. Put a two-centimeter bracket against the side of the clay. Press a shell straight down and lift it straight up. Point into the hollow print and label it ‘Mold.’

scenes.tts: Make some prints while your child looks away. Swap plates and ask, “What made this print?” Then ask, “What clue helped you guess?” Match the prints to the objects. A ridged scallop shell points to the sea. A leaf points to land with plants.

scenes.visual: Swap two paper plates on the tabletop. Show a scallop shell and a leaf sliding next to their matching clay prints. Trace a ridge and a vein on each object and its print when the parent checks the guesses.
scenes.narration: Make some prints while your child looks away. Swap plates and ask, “What made this print?” Then ask, “What clue helped you guess?” Match the prints to the objects. A ridged scallop shell points to the sea. A leaf points to land with plants.

scenes.tts: Try a quick prediction before your next print. Use a ridged shell and a leaf with thick veins. Which details do you think will still show up after you lift the objects away?
scenes.caption: Try a quick prediction before your next print. Use a ridged shell and a leaf with thick veins. Which details do you think will still show up after you lift the objects away?
scenes.visual: On the same tabletop, show the raised ridges of a scallop shell and the thick veins of a leaf over two blank clay discs. Leave both discs blank. Show the question ‘Which details will stay?’
scenes.narration: Try a quick prediction before your next print. Use a ridged shell and a leaf with thick veins. Which details do you think will still show up after you lift the objects away?

scenes.visual: Hold the shell, leaf, and blank clay discs with the question ‘Which details will stay?’ on screen for the full silent pause. Use a slowly moving ring to mark the pause.

scenes.tts: Press and lift each object. Compare the shell ridges and leaf veins with their hollow prints. In Virginia, fossil scallops in river cliffs show that a shallow sea once covered that land. The scallops lived in the sea.
scenes.caption: Press and lift each object. Compare the shell ridges and leaf veins with their hollow prints. In Virginia, fossil scallops in river cliffs show that a shallow sea once covered that land. The scallops lived in the sea.
scenes.visual: Press the shell and leaf straight down into separate clay discs and lift both straight up. Trace the matching ridges and veins. Carry the shell shape into a schematic river-cliff cross-section with fossil scallops in layers of shelly sand. Briefly show a shallow sea over the same land.

scenes.tts: If you choose to make a cast, only an adult handles the plaster. Work outdoors or by a wide-open window. Keep children and pets away. Wear a NIOSH-approved dust mask, eye protection, and gloves. Never put any body part in plaster. It can get hot.
scenes.caption: If you choose to make a cast, only an adult handles the plaster. Work outdoors or by a wide-open window. Keep children and pets away. Wear a NIOSH-approved dust mask, eye protection, and gloves. Never put any body part in plaster. It can get hot.
scenes.visual: Keep the clay mold on the tabletop. At an outdoor work surface, show only the adult putting on a NIOSH-approved dust mask, eye protection, and gloves before opening the bag. Show the child and pets well away from the work surface. Use heat waves over setting plaster and a crossed-out hand.

scenes.tts: Build a clay wall about two centimeters high. Mix the plaster as directed and pour it into the mold. Keep children back until it cools. It hardens in about thirty to sixty minutes. Leave it overnight to dry. Then peel off the clay to see the raised cast.
scenes.caption: Build a clay wall about two centimeters high. Mix the plaster as directed and pour it into the mold. Keep children back until it cools. It hardens in about thirty to sixty minutes. Leave it overnight to dry. Then peel off the clay to see the raised cast.
scenes.visual: Show the protected adult wrapping a clay wall around the mold, mixing plaster in a disposable cup as directed on the package, and filling the mold. Show the plaster cooling, then a night-to-morning transition. Show the adult peeling the clay from the dry cast. Set it beside a separate hollow mold and label each.

scenes.tts: For ages five to seven, skip the plaster and sort prints into water and land. For ages eight to ten, try a sand dig. Use lightly damp play sand below face height. Bury shells, leaf prints, or hardened casts. Brush gently and keep the sand in the tub. Wash hands with soap and water when you finish. Your child used shapes as clues, just as scientists do with fossils.

An adult oversees gentle brushing with a paintbrush. Show soap and water at cleanup, then return to the shell print beside its matching shell.
